Shetland: Britain's Most Northerly Motorcycle Adventure

Shetland lies closer to Norway than to Edinburgh, and it shows. These islands have a distinctly Norse character — Viking heritage, dramatic sea cliffs, and a rugged beauty that feels more Scandinavian than Scottish. Riding here is a genuine adventure — you're at the very edge of Britain, and the sense of remoteness is intoxicating.

Getting There

NorthLink Ferries operates an overnight sailing from Aberdeen to Lerwick, departing at 5pm and arriving at 7:30am. It's a proper sea voyage across the North Sea — 12.5 hours through waters that can be lively. The ship has comfortable cabins, a restaurant, and a bar. Book a cabin — the crossing is too long to sit up all night. Alternatively, fly to Sumburgh Airport and hire a bike locally.

The Riding Experience

Shetland's roads are well-maintained and virtually empty. The main A970 runs the length of the Mainland from Sumburgh Head to Toft (about 55 miles), and inter-island ferries connect to Yell, Unst, Whalsay, and other islands. The total road network is about 500 miles — enough for 2-3 full days of riding. Traffic is virtually non-existent outside Lerwick.

Must-See Shetland

  • Sumburgh Head — Puffin colony at the southern tip, with a lighthouse and views to Fair Isle
  • Jarlshof — 4,000 years of habitation from Bronze Age to Viking Norse, one of Europe's most remarkable archaeological sites
  • St Ninian's Isle — Connected by Britain's finest tombolo (sand bar), with a buried Viking treasure hoard
  • Eshaness — Volcanic sea cliffs on the west coast, spectacularly dramatic in wind
  • Unst — Britain's most northerly inhabited island, with Muckle Flugga lighthouse
Shetland is not for everyone — it's remote, windswept, and a long way from anywhere. But for motorcyclists who crave genuine adventure and empty roads, it's paradise.

Unst: The Final Frontier

Reaching Unst — Britain's most northerly inhabited island — requires two short ferry crossings (Mainland to Yell, Yell to Unst). The reward is riding to the end of Britain — past the Hermaness National Nature Reserve to views of Muckle Flugga lighthouse and Out Stack, the UK's most northerly point. There's a bus shelter at Baltasound decorated by locals — a quirky landmark.

Practical Information

Lerwick has all facilities including fuel, supermarkets, and accommodation. Elsewhere, fuel is available in Brae, Walls, and Sandwick. Weather is Shetland's biggest challenge — wind is constant and can be very strong. Rain is frequent. The islands enjoy long summer days (nearly 24 hours of light in June) and dramatic northern lights in winter. Pack warm, waterproof gear regardless of season. faq.q: How do I get to Shetland by motorcycle?
faq.a: NorthLink Ferries operates an overnight sailing from Aberdeen to Lerwick, departing at 5pm and arriving at 7:30am. It is a proper 12.5-hour sea voyage across the North Sea, so book a cabin rather than sitting up all night. Alternatively, fly to Sumburgh Airport and hire a bike locally.

faq.q: What is the riding like on Shetland?
faq.a: Shetland's roads are well-maintained and virtually empty. The main A970 runs the length of the Mainland from Sumburgh Head to Toft, about 55 miles, and inter-island ferries connect to Yell, Unst, Whalsay and others. The total network is around 500 miles, enough for two to three full days of riding, with almost no traffic outside Lerwick.

faq.q: How do I reach Unst, the most northerly island?
faq.a: Reaching Unst requires two short ferry crossings, first from the Mainland to Yell and then from Yell to Unst. The reward is riding to the end of Britain, past the Hermaness National Nature Reserve to views of Muckle Flugga lighthouse and Out Stack, the UK's most northerly point.

faq.q: Where can I get fuel and stay?
faq.a: Lerwick has all facilities including fuel, supermarkets and accommodation. Elsewhere, fuel is available in Brae, Walls and Sandwick. Plan your fuel stops carefully given the distances and the ferry crossings between islands.

faq.q: What should I expect from the weather?
faq.a: Wind is Shetland's biggest challenge and is constant, sometimes very strong, so ride with care. Rain is frequent. The islands enjoy long summer days with nearly 24 hours of light in June, and dramatic northern lights in winter. Pack warm, waterproof gear regardless of season.
